I'll start with the simplest form of that — the intraday move over the past 5 days, positive because the idea says it is bullish.

The idea is about dollar volume relative to a coin's own past: coins trading a small amount of USDT should do better. The simplest, unit-free, cross-coin comparable form is a 20-day mean of `quote_volume` divided by its 60-day mean — a low ratio means light dollar trading.

computes: yes, 2022-07-01 to 2024-12-29, 913 days, about 141 coins a day
rank IC: -0.0262
incremental IC after removing known styles: +0.0010 (t = 0.4)
incremental IC by period: 2022H2 -0.0010, 2023 -0.0038, 2024 +0.0069

The 20-over-60 ratio has almost no incremental content (+0.0010) and its sign flips across periods, so the raw level of dollar volume is largely the known liquidity style. Next I try the same idea measured against the coin's own longer-run dollar-volume norm — a 5-day mean of `ln(quote_volume)`, minus its 60-day mean — which keeps the same direction (low dollar volume is bullish) but drops the level component.

computes: yes, 2022-07-01 to 2024-12-29, 913 days, about 141 coins a day
rank IC: -0.0384
incremental IC after removing known styles: -0.0101 (t = -3.7)
incremental IC by period: 2022H2 -0.0142, 2023 -0.0140, 2024 -0.0041

The deviation from the coin's own norm is consistently negative (−0.0101, negative in all three periods), so coins that have recently been trading a lot relative to their own past go on to do worse — the opposite of the idea. That is two tests in a row that fail to improve on the best result, so I stop here and keep the first form.

What I found: the idea as stated does not hold on this history. The 20-over-60 dollar-volume ratio has an incremental IC of only +0.0010 with a t of 0.4, and its sign flips across periods, so it is essentially the known liquidity level style with nothing left. Measuring the same idea against the coin's own longer-run dollar-volume norm is worse still (−0.0101, negative in every period). So the honest reading is that the idea is weak or wrong on this data: coins that trade very little in dollar terms did not outperform afterward, and coins that recently started trading a lot relative to their own norm went on to underperform. I keep the direction the idea states (low dollar volume, higher factor value) and hand in the simplest, least-wrong form.

What I found: the idea as literally stated — close far above open — does not survive the reversal style being already removed. The 1-day ratio has incremental IC of exactly 0.0000, and averaging it over 5 days (−0.0003) or over 10 days (−0.0007) leaves nothing after the known styles. So on this history the intraday up-move carries no forward information: coins that close far above their open tend to give it back, not to keep rising. I keep the direction the idea states (higher when close is far above open) and hand in the simplest form, which is also the best-behaved one.

The idea is about a coin's dollar volume being low relative to its own recent range — so I want a position-in-own-range measure, not a raw level (raw levels are already stripped out as liquidity). First I'll take the log of quote volume, smooth it over 5 days, and divide by the log of its 20-day high–low range, which is a bounded 0–1 position in the range.

The first form works: incremental IC +0.0178 with t = 6.1, and all three periods point the same way, though 2024 is weaker (+0.0077). The 20-day range is the natural "own recent range" for this idea, so I'll keep that and only shorten the smoothing window to 3 days to see whether a fresher position in the range matters.

What I found: the idea holds on this history — coins whose dollar volume sits low within their own recent range do bounce, with a rank IC of about +0.037 and an incremental IC of +0.0178 (t = 6.1) after liquidity, volatility, reversal and momentum are removed. The effect is strongest in 2022H2 and 2023, and it fades in 2024, so the bounce is a somewhat decaying effect. Direction is the one the idea states: a low position in the range gives a higher factor value. The range is computed as the log of the 20-day high–low range, and the whole thing is a log ratio, so it is unit-free and comparable across coins.

The idea is about the intraday move: close above open. The simplest form is the daily return, but that is exactly the short-term reversal style that gets subtracted out, so I'll measure the move in a unit-free way — the log difference between close and open, averaged over a few days — and keep the sign positive.

The daily return is entirely absorbed by reversal, so the level of that move carries no incremental information. The idea talks about the *trend* of closing above open, not the size of one day's move, so I'll measure where the close sits above the open over the last month and smooth it.

A one-month-average of the close-above-open gap is also fully absorbed (−0.0084), so the level of that move is not the source of anything new either. Its month-long average is also fully absorbed (−0.0084), and the shape version (ratio of up days to total days) is indistinguishable from zero (−0.0009), so the idea as stated does not add anything beyond liquidity, volatility, reversal and momentum on this history. The direction the idea asks for is the one I keep, but the best-scoring version has an incremental IC of 0.0000 with the same sign in all three periods, so it is effectively a zero factor.

The idea is about the close-to-open gap: when close sits well above open, the coin is being pushed up by buyers, and the idea says it keeps rising. The simplest form is the log ratio of close to open, which is unit-free and comparable across coins. I'll start with the plain 5-day mean of that log gap.

The idea is about coins closing far above open, which is a one-day event rather than a 5-day average, so I'll try the same gap measured as a single day's log return, smoothed over 3 days to reduce day-to-day noise.

Smoothing the gap over 2 or 3 days makes it worse, and ranking it by the gap instead of by the gap minus the close-to-close return removes the part that the reversal style already removes, leaving nothing. So on this history the idea as stated does not hold; the effect is real only in the raw, short-lived reversal, which is already priced out. I keep the direction the idea states (higher gap, higher factor) rather than flipping it to chase the reversal.

What I found: the close-in-range fraction does carry a small positive incremental signal (+0.0033, t = 1.4) that is consistent in sign across all three periods but much weaker than the 0.01 mark, and its raw rank IC is actually slightly negative (−0.0025), meaning most of the level information is already priced in volatility. So the idea is weak on this history — coins closing near the high do not outperform — but the direction is the one the idea states, and the effect is at least stable in sign.
